1.text: **Detergent action:** surfactant molecules orient their hydrophobic part toward the fat or dirt particle and their hydrophilic part toward water; surface tension falls, wetting improves, and the fat passes into micelles and is washed away with water. Cationic surfactants, in turn, adsorb on the negatively charged membrane of microbes and disrupt it — that is why they are antiseptics.

parts.text: If **cationic antiseptics** (benzalkonium chloride, chlorhexidine) are used together with anionic soap, the oppositely charged ions bind to each other and the antiseptic is **inactivated**. That is why hands washed with soap are rinsed thoroughly before the antiseptic is applied.

4.text: Langmuir’s theory is valid only for a single layer. Vapors and gases near their condensation temperature adsorb on a surface in **many layers** — this is described by the **BET theory** (Brunauer–Emmett–Teller); the method is used to determine the specific surface area of sorbents.

**Activated charcoal** is the most widely used sorbent in acute oral poisoning. Adults are usually given 50 g (about 1 g/kg) as a suspension in water; it is most effective if given **within 1 hour** of ingestion. Charcoal adsorbs large, nonpolar or weakly polar molecules well.

6.text: In column chromatography each substance leaves the column at its own time — it is identified by its **retention time**, and its amount is found from the peak area. **Chromatography–mass spectrometry** identifies the substances separated by chromatography precisely by their mass spectrum: it is used in forensic toxicology, doping control and the **newborn screening** for inherited metabolic diseases (dozens of amino acids and acylcarnitines in a single dried blood spot).

The **amino acid analyzer** uses ion-exchange chromatography: amino acids leave a cation-exchange column one after another according to their charge and the pH and are determined quantitatively with ninhydrin. **Affinity chromatography** is based on specific binding: if an antigen is attached to the column, only the matching antibody is retained from the mixture.

blocks.text: When a drop of liquid touches a solid surface, its shape depends on the ratio of **cohesion** (attraction between liquid molecules) and **adhesion** (attraction between liquid and solid molecules). This is assessed by the **contact angle** θ: θ < 90° — the surface is wetted by the liquid (**hydrophilic** surface: glass, quartz, protein), θ > 90° — it is not wetted (**hydrophobic** surface: paraffin, fat, Teflon).

In a narrow tube a wetting liquid forms a concave meniscus and rises, while a non-wetting liquid falls. **Jurin’s formula:** h = 2σ·cosθ / (ρ·g·r), where r is the radius of the capillary. The narrower the capillary, the higher the liquid rises.

items: When blood is taken from a finger, glass capillaries and test strips draw up blood by **capillary forces**.
Cotton and gauze dressings absorb wound discharge through the capillaries between hydrophilic fibers.
The movement of liquid in soil, paper and tissues and the rise of the solvent in paper chromatography are also based on capillarity.

parts.text: **Gas embolism:** an air bubble that enters a small vessel is deformed where the vessel narrows; because the menisci at its two ends have different curvature, an opposing pressure arises and the bubble blocks the blood flow (the **Jamin effect**). That is why air is always removed from the system during intravenous injections and infusions.

blocks.text: In many analytical and staining methods the color or precipitate observed is not a simple chemical reaction but the result of **selective adsorption** of a dye or ion on the surface of a precipitate (a colloidal particle, a fiber).

parts.text: The key to how an adsorption indicator works is the **change in the sign of the particle charge**: before the equivalence point the precipitate adsorbs the excess ion being determined (Cl^−^), after it — the excess titrant (Ag^+^) (Paneth–Fajans rule).

skills.title: Skill: determination of chlorides by the Fajans method

items: Pipette 10 mL of the test solution (for example, diluted normal saline) into a flask.
Add 2–3 drops of fluorescein (or eosin) solution; the medium should be neutral or weakly acidic.
Add 0.1 M AgNO~3~ dropwise from a burette with stirring: a white AgCl precipitate forms, and the solution has a yellow-green fluorescence.
Stop the titration as soon as the surface of the precipitate suddenly turns **pink** — this is the equivalence point.
Calculate the chloride content: C(Cl^−^) = C(AgNO~3~)·V(AgNO~3~) / V(sample).

cases.title: Problem 4
cases.text: The adsorption of acetic acid on charcoal was studied: at an equilibrium concentration of 0.01 mol/L x / m = 0.2 mmol/g, at 0.1 mol/L x / m = 0.5 mmol/g.
cases.ask: Find the constants of the Freundlich equation (1/n and K).
cases.answer: lg(x / m) = lgK + (1 / n)·lgC. Two points: lg0.2 = −0.70, lgC = −2; lg0.5 = −0.30, lgC = −1. Slope: 1 / n = (−0.30 − (−0.70)) / (−1 − (−2)) = **0.4**. lgK = −0.30 − 0.4 · (−1) = 0.10, K ≈ **1.26** mmol/g (C in mol/L). 1/n < 1 — as concentration increases, adsorption increases more slowly (the surface begins to saturate).

cases.title: Problem 5
cases.text: Two patients were brought to the toxicology department within one hour: the first (70 kg) had taken 40 carbamazepine tablets, the second had taken iron sulfate tablets.
cases.ask: Which patient will benefit from activated charcoal and at what dose? Why is it useless for the second patient, and what is done for them?
cases.answer: **Carbamazepine** is a large, weakly polar molecule that adsorbs well on charcoal: the first patient is given ≈ 1 g/kg, that is **50–70 g** of charcoal as a suspension in water (less than 1 hour has passed since ingestion — the most effective time). **Iron** ions are small and charged and hardly adsorb on charcoal — charcoal is useless for the second patient. For them, gastrointestinal decontamination (if indicated), measurement of blood iron and, in severe cases, the chelator **deferoxamine** are used.

cases.title: Problem 6
cases.text: A glass capillary with an inner radius of 0.1 mm is used to take blood from a finger. For water σ = 0.073 N/m, ρ = 1000 kg/m^3^, θ ≈ 0°.
cases.ask: To what height does water rise in the capillary? How does the result change for blood?
cases.answer: h = 2σ·cosθ / (ρ·g·r) = 2 · 0.073 · 1 / (1000 · 9.81 · 0.0001) = 0.146 / 0.981 ≈ **0.15 m** (15 cm). The surface tension of blood (≈ 0.05 N/m) is lower than that of water and its density slightly higher, so it rises less, but this is still enough to fill a capillary a few centimeters long — the capillary “draws up” the blood by itself.

cases.title: Problem 7
cases.text: A nurse washed her hands with anionic soap and, without rinsing, immediately applied an antiseptic solution containing benzalkonium chloride. Later, infections transmitted by hands increased in the ward.
cases.ask: Explain from a physicochemical point of view why the antiseptic may have been ineffective.
cases.answer: Benzalkonium chloride is a **cationic** surfactant: its positively charged polar group adsorbs on the negatively charged surface of the microbial membrane and disrupts it. Soap is an **anionic** substance. Soap anions left on the hands bind to the antiseptic cations to form a neutral, poorly active compound — the antiseptic is **inactivated**. The correct sequence is: wash with soap → rinse thoroughly with running water → dry → apply the antiseptic.

cases.title: Problem 8
cases.text: A kidney biopsy from a patient with a chronic suppurative disease was stained with Congo red. Under an ordinary microscope pink-red masses were seen, and in polarized light an apple-green glow.
cases.ask: What diagnosis is suspected? On what physicochemical phenomenon is the staining based?
cases.answer: This is **amyloidosis** (secondary AA amyloidosis in chronic inflammation). Congo red is a dye with linear molecules; it **adsorbs in an ordered, oriented way** on the surface of the β-pleated sheets of amyloid fibrils. Because the dye molecules line up in one direction, the preparation becomes birefringent and glows **apple-green** in polarized light — a specific sign of amyloid.
